rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Most reciters divide stopping into four classes—complete, sufficient, good, and improper; some reduce them to three by omitting the good, and others to two by omitting sufficient and good.
rows.anchor: والوقف عند أكثر القراء ينقسم إلى أربعة أقسام تام مختار وكاف جائز وحسن مفهوم وقبيح متروك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A complete stop has no syntactic or semantic attachment to what follows and permits a fresh start; a sufficient stop is detached in wording but remains connected in meaning, as after this phrase.
rows.anchor: منقطع فى اللفظ متعلق فى المعنى فيحسن الوقف عليه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Complete stops most often fall at verse endings, but may occur before a verse ends or after its end when the next phrase attaches by meaning; ends of narratives and sūras are complete stops.
rows.anchor: وقد يوجد قبل انقضاء الفاصلة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The passage lists further usual complete-stop locations, including before vocative particles, commands, oaths and their lām, and after verse endings, unless a preceding statement or oath governs them.
rows.anchor: وقبل ياء النداء وفعل الأمر والقسم ولامه دون القول والله بعد رأس كل آية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Many constructions generally allow a sufficient stop, including a verse head followed by lām of purpose, exception meaning ‘but,’ emphatic إن, questions, بل, and certain future or response particles; preceding speech or an oath can alter the judgment.
rows.anchor: وكل رأس آية بعدها لام كى وإلا بمعنى لكن وإن المكسورة المشددة والاستفهام وبل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some grammarians count only five instances of the light/open إن construction: three in al-Baqara, one in al-Nisāʾ, and one in al-Nūr.
rows.anchor: وقيل أن المفتوحة المخففة خمسة لا غير

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The account says the phrase about the final creation stage in 23:14 occasioned the apostasy of ʿAbd Allāh b. Abī Sarḥ: while dictating it, he claimed the wording had occurred to him and that he too was a prophet.
rows.anchor: قال رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم اكتب

words: ومن أظلم ممن افترى على الله كذبا
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The source reports that this verse was revealed about ʿAbd Allāh b. Abī Sarḥ, ʿUthmān’s foster brother, after his claim that he could reveal like God; he then left Islam.
rows.anchor: نزلت فى عبد الله بن أبى سرح أخى عثمان

words: أو قال أوحي إلي ولم يوح إليه شيء
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase about someone claiming revelation without receiving it is reported as revealed concerning Musaylima the Liar, who claimed that God had revealed to him.
rows.anchor: فإنه نزل فى مسيلمة الكذاب حين زعم أن الله سبحانه أوحى إليه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Anʿām is described as wholly Meccan except six verses, including its final passage beginning ‘Say: Come’; the source says reports established this classification.
rows.anchor: ثلاث آيات من آخرها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Aʿrāf is Meccan except three verses, beginning with the command to ask about the town and extending through the verse about the mountain being raised.
rows.anchor: سورة الأعراف مكية إلا ثلاث آيات

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibrāhīm is classified as Meccan except two verses revealed concerning those killed at Badr.
rows.anchor: نزلتا فى قتلى بدر

words: والذين هاجروا في الله من بعد ما ظلموا
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Naḥl is Meccan up to the verse about those who emigrated after being wronged; the remainder is Medinan.
rows.anchor: سورة النحل مكية إلى قوله

words: وإن كادوا ليفتنونك عن الذي أوحينا إليك
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sūra of Banī Isrāʾīl is Meccan apart from the passage about nearly tempting the Prophet away from revelation, which concerns Thaqīf and has its own story.
rows.anchor: يعنى ثقيفا وله قصة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Kahf is Meccan except the command to keep oneself with the believers, which was revealed concerning Salmān al-Fārisī.
rows.anchor: نزلت فى سلمان الفارسى وله قصة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Qaṣaṣ is Meccan except a verse about people given scripture before the Qurʾān; it concerns forty believing People of the Book who came from Abyssinia with Jaʿfar and converted.
rows.anchor: نزلت فى أربعين رجلا من مؤمنى أهل الكتاب قدموا من الحبشة مع جعفر بن أبى طالب فأسلموا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: An with its clause can occupy the accusative object position, as in ‘God intends to lighten [the burden] for you.’
rows.anchor: يريد الله أن يخفف عنكم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The source catalogs أن-clauses in nominative positions as subjects and predicates, and as the grammatical subject of a verb, illustrating each use with Qurʾanic examples.
rows.anchor: فالمبتدأ يكون في موضع رفع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In ‘We sent Noah … that he warn,’ أن is understood with an omitted preposition (بأن), whose deletion lets the verb govern the clause directly.
rows.anchor: معناه بأن انذر فلما حذفت الباء تعدي الفعل فنصب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One grammatical analysis makes أن اعبدوا accusative as an apposition to ‘what You commanded me.’
rows.anchor: نصب على البدل من قوله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After a preposition, أن and its clause can form a genitive verbal noun, as in ‘before your coming’; the source also notes that the preposition may be omitted in other constructions.
rows.anchor: فيكون في موضع جر

rows.speaker: سيبويه
rows.claim: For the omitted-preposition construction in ‘that they be left to say,’ Sibawayh analyzes the clause as accusative, whereas al-Khalīl rejects that and retains the original genitive analysis.
rows.anchor: ومذهب سيبويه انها في موضع نصب ونفاها الخليل على اصل الجر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After ʿasā, the clause is interpreted as an accusative verbal noun when ʿasā is incomplete, and as nominative when it is complete; Qurʾanic examples illustrate both constructions.
rows.anchor: فتكون مع صلتها في تاويل مصدر منصوب إن كانت ناقصة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The lām in ‘he is intense in love of wealth’ is causal, equivalent to ‘because of’ (من أجل).
rows.anchor: وللتعليل وهي التي يصلح موضعها من أجل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The lām in the Quraysh opening is connected either to ‘let them worship’ or to the preceding clause; this linkage explains why Ubayy’s codex treated the passages as one sūra. Linking it to the destruction is criticized, and an omitted ‘wonder!’ is also proposed.
rows.anchor: ولهذا كانتا في مصحف أبي سورة واحدة

rows.speaker: الراغب
rows.claim: Al-Rāghib reads the lām as ‘on behalf of/because of the traitors’: do not litigate for them. He equates it with ‘do not argue for those who betray themselves,’ unlike ‘be an adversary of God.’
rows.anchor: وليست كالتي في قولك لا تكن لله خصيما

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The source gives examples where lām is used with the sense of ‘to/until,’ including the statement that the sun and moon run to a specified term, supported by ‘He will defer you until a stated term.’
rows.anchor: هذا قول الزمخشري وهو أولى من قول غيره إنها بمعنى إلى

rows.speaker: الراغب
rows.claim: Al-Rāghib rejects treating the lām in God’s inspiration to the bee as the same as prophetic revelation ‘to’ someone: the bee is given this by subjection and inspiration, so lām marks what is assigned to it.
rows.anchor: وزيفه الراغب لأن الوحي للنحل جعل ذلك له للتسخير والإلهام وليس كالوحي الموحى إلى الأنبياء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The lām can carry the sense ‘upon,’ as in falling upon the chins or laying Isaac down upon his forehead.
rows.anchor: أي فعليها لأن السيئة على الإنسان لا له

words: وإن أحسنتم أحسنتم لأنفسكم وإن أسأتم فلها
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In ‘if you do evil, it is for it,’ lām means ‘against’ (عليها), since wrongdoing falls upon the wrongdoer; the source adduces verses that explicitly say ‘against oneself.’
rows.anchor: أي فعليها لأن السيئة على الإنسان لا له

words: ولو أن قرآنا سيرت به الجبال
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The apodosis of this conditional is omitted; the most common estimate is ‘they would not believe,’ making the clause say they would fail to believe even if the Qurʾān moved mountains.
rows.anchor: ونقل الشيخ محيي الدين النووي في كتاب رءوس المسائل كون الجواب كان هذا القرآن عن الأكثرين

words: ولو أن قرآنا سيرت به الجبال
rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: Al-Farrāʾ instead takes the answer as advanced before the condition: ‘they disbelieve in the Merciful, even if a Qurʾān moved the mountains.’
rows.anchor: سيرت به الجبال وهذا قول الفراء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One reconstruction supplies ‘the pens and seas would be exhausted’ before the stated denial that God’s words would not be exhausted; another treats the denial itself as the apodosis, intensifying the assertion of inexhaustibility.
rows.anchor: والتقدير لنفدت هذه الاشياء وما نفدت كلمات الله ويحتمل أن يكون ما نفدت هو الجواب مبالغة في نفي النفاد

words: ولولا فضل الله عليك ورحمته لهمت طائفة منهم أن يضلوك
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The surface reading appears to deny that the group intended to mislead the Prophet, contrary to the account that they did intend it and advanced their claim.
rows.anchor: فإنه قد قيل ظاهره نفى وجود الهم منهم بإضلاله وهو خلاف الواقع فإنهم هموا وردوا القول

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: An alternative analysis takes ‘they intended’ as a preposed oath-like statement, with the conditional answer omitted: without God’s favor, they would have misled you.
rows.anchor: ليس جواب لو بل هو كلام تقدم على لو وجوابها مقول على طريق القسم

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī supplies an omitted answer to the conditional: had Joseph not seen his Lord’s proof, he would have consorted with her.
rows.anchor: ذكره أبو البقاء والأول للزمخشري

rows.speaker: أبو البقاء
rows.claim: Abū al-Baqāʾ offers the alternative that Joseph would have desired her if he had not seen the proof; on this reading the stop is after ‘she desired him,’ and Joseph did not desire her.
rows.anchor: ذكره أبو البقاء والأول للزمخشري

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A conditional’s answer cannot be placed before the conditional because the conditional, as a condition, has precedence in the sentence.
rows.anchor: ولا يجوز تقديم جواب لو عليها لأنه في حكم الشرط وللشرط صدر الكلام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The answer is omitted but supplied by the repeated phrase ‘we will be guided’; the inserted condition interrupts the clause, and its position highlights that guidance depends on God’s will.
rows.anchor: جواب الشرط محذوف يدل عليه

words: وما أوتيتم من العلم إلا قليلا
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One report says Jews challenged the Prophet’s statement that people had little knowledge, citing the Torah’s divine words, rulings, light, and guidance; he replied that the Torah was little of much, and the verse about the sea as ink was revealed.
rows.anchor: سببها أن اليهود جاءوا إلى النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم

words: ولو أنما في الأرض من شجرة أقلام
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A second report assigns the revelation instead to the verse comparing all earthly trees to pens and the seas to ink.
rows.anchor: ولو أنما في الأرض من شجرة أقلام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The commentators say the point is that God’s words are innumerable; the verse makes this comprehensible by comparing them with finite quantities, the greatest abundance people know.
rows.anchor: والغرض من ذلك الإعلام بكثرة كلماته وهي في نفسها غير متناهية وإنما قرب الأمر على أفهام البشر

rows.speaker: بعض المحققين
rows.claim: Some careful scholars say the verse asserts that God’s words would not run out, without asserting that even the imagined pens and seas could exhaust them; the source compares this with al-Khiḍr’s bird-and-sea analogy for divine knowledge.
rows.anchor: وقال بعض المحققين إن ما تضمنت الآية أن كلمات الله تعالى لم تكن لتنفد ولم تقتض الآية أنها تنفد

words: خذ العفو وأمر بالعرف وأعرض عن الجاهلين
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The source groups overlooking faults, forgiving sins, ignoring slips, and concealing honorable people’s lapses with this rhetorical hyperbole; one gloss says it means maintaining ties, giving to those who withhold, and forgiving wrongdoers.
rows.anchor: وعد بعضهم من هذا القبيل ما جاء من المبالغة في القرآن من الإغضاء عن العيوب والصفح عن الذنوب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Explicitly stating a cause is more emphatic than giving a ruling without its cause: the named cause supports generalizing the effect, and people are more inclined to transmit rulings whose rationale is stated.
rows.anchor: بأن يذكر الشيء معللا فإنه أبلغ من ذكره بلا علة لوجهين أحدهما أن العلة المنصوصة قاضية بعموم المعلول

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Most Qurʾanic causal clauses answer an unstated ‘why?’ prompted by the preceding statement; the causal sense is evident because a causal فاء could replace إن here.
rows.anchor: وغالب التعليل في القرآن فهو على تقدير جواب سؤال اقتضته الجملة الأولى وهو سؤال عن العلة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The source identifies ‘wisdom’ as beneficial knowledge and righteous action, and presents the named wisdom as an explicit rationale or purpose marker.
rows.anchor: والحكمة هي العلم النافع والعمل الصالح

words: فالتقطه آل فرعون ليكون لهم عدوا وحزنا
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Although some take the lām as an unintended outcome, the source argues that divine acts carry wisdom though they are not compelled by it; an outcome lām applies to someone ignorant of consequences, not to God.
rows.anchor: فالجواب أن معنى قولنا إن أفعال الله تعالى لا تعلل أي لا تجب ولكنها لا تخلو عن الحكمة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The lām is a lām of wisdom and intended purpose: the verse explains God’s decree and arrangement that they take him in; mentioning their action rather than the decree heightens their sorrow and regret.
rows.anchor: وأما من هو بكل شيء عليم فمستحيله في حقه وإنما اللام الواردة في أحكامه وأفعاله لام الحكمة والغاية المطلوبة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God’s answer to the angels’ question about corruption presupposes wisdom and interests known to Him; otherwise neither their question about His wisdom nor this answer would make sense.
rows.anchor: سبحانه مجردا عن الحكم والغايات

rows.speaker: أبو إسحاق الإسفرابيني
rows.claim: When two verses conflict, al-Isfarāyīnī says to establish their chronology and treat the later as abrogating the earlier; if chronology is unknown, consensus on using one identifies the abrogating verse. He says no Qurʾanic pair lacks these indicators.
rows.anchor: قال الأستاذ أبو إسحاق الإسفرابيني

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One proposed priority test uses Meccan and Medinan classification as a chronology cue: exceptions are possible, but most Meccan verses preceded the Hijra, so the Medinan ruling is generally later for specification and priority.
rows.anchor: وإن كان يجوز أن تكون المكية نزلت عليه صلى الله عليه وسلم بعد عوده إلى مكة والمدنية قبلها فيقدم الحكم بالآية المدنية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Where one rule reflects the prevalent conditions of Mecca and another those of Medina, the source prefers the Medinan context; the general promise of sanctuary can be qualified for someone liable to retaliation.
rows.anchor: فيقدم الحكم بالخبر الذي فيه أحول أهل المدينة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The prohibition on killing game in the sanctuary is reconciled with the permissibility of trained hunting animals: game caught inside the sanctuary remains prohibited, while game caught outside and brought in alive is excepted.
rows.anchor: فجعل النهي فيمن اصطاده في الحرم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: When one text states a rule independently and the other requires adding an unstated rule, the independent command to complete pilgrimage prevails; consensus says the offering is not obligatory merely because one is prevented.
rows.anchor: وقد أجمعت الأمة على أن الهدي لا يجب بنفس الحصر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The idiom of rolling up one’s shins originated in facing a grave task that requires exertion, and figuratively conveys hardship.
rows.anchor: وأصل هذا أن الرجل إذا وقع في أمر عظيم يحتاج إلى معاناة

rows.speaker: اللغويون
rows.claim: The language scholars gloss ‘in God’s side’ as ‘in obedience to and command of God’: neglect cannot occur in a bodily side, so the phrase should not be taken as attributing limbs to God.
rows.anchor: قال اللغويون معناه ما فرطت في طاعة الله وأمره لأن التفريط لا يقع إلا في ذلك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Faragha can mean to finish a task or turn one’s attention to someone; here it means God will attend to punishing the two communities and determining their recompense.
rows.anchor: فرغ يأتي بمعنى قطع شغلا أتفرغ لك أي أقصد قصدك والآية منه أي سنقصد لعقوبتكم ونحكم جزاءكم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One reading assigns ‘I think him a liar’ to Pharaoh, continuous with his preceding words; another places the stop earlier and takes ظن as certain knowledge rather than doubt, as in ‘I was certain I would meet my account.’
rows.anchor: أحدهما أن يكون الظن لفرعون وهو شك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Negating drowsiness and sleep does not ascribe wakefulness or movement to God, since ‘awake’ presupposes having slept; the intended sense is freedom from ignorance and inattention.
rows.anchor: لم يرد سبحانه بنفي النوم والسنة عن نفسه إثبات اليقظة والحركة لأنه لا يقال لله تعالى يقظان ولا نائم

rows.speaker: السهيلي
rows.claim: Al-Suhaylī says ‘hand’ is originally an expression for an attribute, as praise of people with hands and eyes concerns qualities, not limbs; this supports affirming the scriptural attribute without specifying a figurative interpretation or bodily form.
rows.anchor: قال السهيلي اليد في الأصل كالمصدر عبارة عن صفة لموصوف ولذلك مدح سبحانه وتعالى بالأيدي مقرونة مع الإبصار

rows.speaker: الأشعري
rows.claim: Al-Ashʿarī’s position, as presented through al-Suhaylī, affirms the two hands as a revealed attribute, neither reducing them to power or blessing nor adopting anthropomorphism.
rows.anchor: قال وإذا ثبت هذا فصح قول الأشعري

words: أم لهم أعين يبصرون بها أم لهم آذان يسمعون بها
rows.speaker: ابن المنير
rows.claim: Ibn al-Munīr rejects the correction made by al-Aṣmaʿī, Khalaf al-Aḥmar, and Ibn Rashīq, and says Jarīr was right: his line meant a day of good without any evil; before can itself negate.
rows.anchor: قال ابن المنير ووقع لي أن الأصمعي وخلف الأحمر وابن رشيق أخطئوا جميعا وأصاب جرير وحده

words: أم لهم أعين يبصرون بها أم لهم آذان يسمعون بها
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The passage illustrates denying a necessary concomitant to deny its subject: the rhetorical questions about idols’ eyes and ears in fact deny that they possess the organs at all.
rows.anchor: فإن ظاهره نفي هذه الجوارح والحقيقة توجب نفي الآية عمن يكون له فضلا عمن لا يكون

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In the prohibition against obeying parents who urge associating partners with God, ‘that of which you have no knowledge’ denies both the alleged object and any knowledge of it.
rows.anchor: وإن جاهداك على أن تشرك بي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase ‘for which He sent down no authority’ denies both the reality of the alleged partners and the existence of any revealed proof for associating them.
rows.anchor: أي شركاء لا ثبوت لها أصلا ولا أنزل الله بإشراكها حجة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asking whether people inform God of what He does not know denies the thing’s existence, since anything real would necessarily be known to Him.
rows.anchor: أي ما لاثبوت له ولا علم الله متعلقا به نفيا للملزوم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ‘Their repentance will not be accepted’ conveys that they will not repent: the necessary acceptance of repentance is denied to deny the act that would require it.
rows.anchor: أصله لن يتوبوا فلن يكون لهم قبول توبة فأوثر الإلحاق ذهابا إلى انتفاء الملزوم بانتفاء اللازم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The chastity condition does not imply that coercion is allowed when enslaved women do not want chastity; coercion is relevant only when they seek chastity, and the verse addressed people doing this.
rows.anchor: معلوم أنه لا إكراه على الفاحشة لمن لا يريد تحصنا لأنها نزلت فيمن يفعل ذلك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The ban on usury applies to small and large amounts, though the verse singles out doubled amounts because that was their practice and the larger amount more sharply condemns them.
rows.anchor: وأكل الربا منهى عنه قليلا وكثيرا لكنها نزلت على سبب وهو فعلهم ذلك ولأنه مقام تشنيع عليهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Tawriya uses a shared word with a near and distant sense, intending the distant one while leading the hearer toward the near; here al-najm means low-growing plants, though the hearer may think of a star, especially after sun and moon.
rows.anchor: وهي أن يتكلم المتكلم بلفظ مشترك بين معنيين قريب وبعيد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The source lists the phrase about standing in prayer in the sanctuary as another example of tawriya, glossing the intended sense as المعرفة.
rows.anchor: وهو قائم يصلي في المحراب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In ‘faces that day are nāʿima,’ the intended sense is that they enjoy blessing and honor, while the hearer may think the faces are smooth.
rows.anchor: أراد بها في نعمة وكرامة والسامع يتوهم أنه أراد من النعومة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The word أيد in the statement that God built the sky means strength, while the hearer may take it to mean hands.
rows.anchor: بأيد ﴾ 4 أراد بالأيد القوة الخارجة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Mukhalladūn is glossed as boys adorned with earrings; the listener may instead infer that they are everlasting.
rows.anchor: أي مقرطون تجعل في آذانهم القرطة والحلق الذي في الأذن يسمى قرطا وخلدة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase means God made the people’s dwellings in Paradise known to them, while the hearer may understand ʿaraf as fragrance.
rows.anchor: أي علمهم منازلهم فيها أو يوهم إرادة العرف الذي هو الطيب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse about trained hunting animals is cited as another example in the list of tawriya, without a further gloss in this passage.
rows.anchor: وما علمتم من الجوارح مكلبين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Mentioning Riḍwān together with gardens may make the hearer think of a garden’s keeper, though the intended word is divine good pleasure.
rows.anchor: فذكر رضوان مع الجنات مما يوهم إرادة خازن الجنات

rows.speaker: أبو جعفر
rows.claim: The Anṣār meant ‘attend to us/listen to us’ by rāʿinā, but unbelievers used it as an insult meaning foolishness; Abū Jaʿfar says it was Hebrew. After the believers’ explanation was challenged, Muslims were forbidden to say it.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو جعفر هي بالعبرانية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One reading takes al-Walī and al-Ḥamīd as divine names: God cares for servants through mercy, and is either a praiser of obedient servants or praised in ease and hardship. Alternatively both refer to rain, the spring rain being walī and praiseworthy.
rows.anchor: ويحتمل أن يكون الولي من أسماء المطر وهو مطر الربيع والحميد بمعنى المحمود وعلى هذا فالضمير عائد على الغيث

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse ‘Who guides to the truth?’ / ‘God guides to the truth’ is offered as a parallel example of a question and answer.
rows.anchor: قل هل من شركائكم من يهدي إلى الحق

rows.speaker: ابن مالك
rows.claim: Answers normally match the question’s clause type, but Ibn Mālik analyzes a short answer such as ‘Zayd’ to ‘Who read?’ as a verbal clause with its verb omitted; complete answers retain the verb, as in the resurrection exchange.
rows.anchor: قال وإنما قدرته كذلك لا مبتدأ مع احتماله

rows.speaker: ابن مالك
rows.claim: The source also uses ‘Say: lawful to you are the good things’ as a full verbal answer; when the final constituent is explicit, a verb is explicit, supporting an omitted verb in abbreviated answers.
rows.anchor: ومما رجح به أيضا تقدير الفعل أنه حيث صرح بالجزء الأخير صرح بالفعل

rows.speaker: ابن يعيش
rows.claim: Ibn Yaʿīsh says an explicit verb is better, but the author rejects this: deletion is more common, and it makes a brief reply unambiguously an answer with a restrictive sense.
rows.anchor: قال ابن يعيش التصريح بالفعل أجود وليس كما زعم بل الأكثر الحذف

rows.speaker: شهاب الدين بن المرحل
rows.claim: Ibn al-Muraḥḥal treats these replies as answering with wording different from the question for a rhetorical point, like the answer about lunar phases; the author says this analysis is questionable.
rows.anchor: فكان الشيخ شهاب الدين بن المرحل رحمه الله يجعله من باب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A short answer like ‘Zayd’ explicitly signals that it answers ‘Who came?’; unlike ‘Zayd came,’ it cannot also stand as an unrelated sentence and conveys the restriction ‘the one who came was Zayd.’
rows.anchor: ولو قلت زيد كان نصا في أنه جواب وفي العموم الذي دلت عليه من وكأنك قلت الذي جاء زيد فيفيد الحصر

words: لمن الملك اليوم لله الواحد القهار
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In ‘To whom belongs sovereignty today? To God,’ the answer omits the subject الملك; the full sense is ‘sovereignty belongs to God alone.’
rows.anchor: إذ التقدير الملك لله الواحد فحذف المبتدأ من الجواب إذ المعنى لا ملك إلا لله
